English translation of the published report. The original R code, including its variable names and comments, is retained.

About this version. The first part preserves the 2021 analysis and the results from the original report. The second includes the corrected review of 2015 and 2019, together with annual trends from 2015 to 2020.

Objective: Conduct a descriptive and exploratory analysis of a dataset.

Dataset: Landings and takeoffs recorded by Empresa Argentina de Navegación Aérea (EANA), Argentina's Ministry of Transport. Detailed records of landings and takeoffs from January 2014 to December 2020.

1 Part One

Assignment instructions

  • Clean the data, checking each variable for errors or unusual cases.
  • Keep domestic flights.
  • The dataset contains airport codes. Add variables for the city, province, and coordinates of each airport. You can find this information in this Wikipedia article. Note: we chose to use the datos_sna dataset provided by the teaching staff, since the Wikipedia data were incomplete.
  • Calculate the distance traveled by each flight. The distHaversine function from the geosphere package may be useful.
  • Calculate the average speed of each flight. To do this, you will need to match different rows in the dataset. The dataset contains takeoffs and landings, which can be used to identify each flight's departure and arrival times.

We load datos_sna, which contains geographic information about the airports used in Part One. We then load the 2021 flight data.

We begin with a basic exploration of the dataset to help clean the data and prepare for the subsequent analysis. First, we examine the flight classification variable, which indicates whether a flight is domestic or international. Given the pandemic, we expect to observe many more domestic flights than international flights. The following table shows the proportions of domestic and international flights.

t <- prop.table(table(datos_2021$`Clasificación Vuelo`))
df_cv <- as.data.frame(t)
round(t,3)
## 
##   Dom Inter 
## 0.898 0.102
ggplot(df_cv, aes(x=Var1, y=Freq)) + 
  coord_flip() +
  geom_col() +
  xlab("Clasificación de vuelo") +
  ylim(0,1) +
  theme_minimal()

Figure 1.1: Proportions of flight classifications in 2021

Figure 1.1 shows that international flights account for a very small proportion of the records, as we expected.

Among domestic flights, we now examine which airports have the most flights, counting both landings and takeoffs:

df_dom <- datos_2021 %>% filter(`Clasificación Vuelo`=="Dom")
t <- prop.table(table(df_dom$Aeropuerto))
df_aer <- as.data.frame(t)
ggplot(df_aer, aes(x=reorder(Var1, Freq), y=Freq)) + 
  geom_col() +
  theme_minimal() +
  xlab("Aeropuertos") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size=6, angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))

Figure 1.2: Domestic flight counts by airport

Figure 1.2 shows that the three airports with the most flights are Morón (MOR), San Fernando (FDO), and Aeroparque (AER). However, most flights arriving at or departing from Morón and San Fernando fall into categories such as non-scheduled, private, and training flights. For our average-speed analysis, we consider only scheduled flights, so these other records are excluded.

datos_2021 %>% 
  filter(Aeropuerto=="MOR"| `Origen / Destino`=="MOR" | Aeropuerto=="FDO" | `Origen / Destino`=="FDO") %>% 
  group_by(`Clase de Vuelo (todos los vuelos)`) %>%
  count(sort=T)

We then carry out an initial cleaning of the dataset, keeping scheduled domestic flights with an airline name recorded. We also add a column for distance traveled, dist_rec_km, in km.

datos_2021 <- datos_2021 %>% 
  filter(`Clasificación Vuelo`=="Dom",
         `Clase de Vuelo (todos los vuelos)`=="Regular", 
         `Aerolinea Nombre`!= 0) %>% 
  select(-c(`Clasificación Vuelo`)) %>% 
  rename(Salida_ANA = Aeropuerto,
         Llegada_ANA = `Origen / Destino`) 

datos_2021 <- left_join(datos_2021, datos_sna[-6], by="Salida_ANA") %>%
  rename(Ciudad.Origen = nom_ciudad, Provincia.Origen = cpr, lat_origen = x, lon_origen = y)

datos_2021 <- left_join(datos_2021, datos_sna[-3], by="Llegada_ANA") %>%
  rename(Ciudad.Destino = nom_ciudad, Provincia.Destino = cpr, lat_destino=x, lon_destino=y)

datos_2021 <- datos_2021 %>% 
  mutate(dist_rec_km = round(distHaversine(p1=cbind(lon_origen, lat_origen),
                                           p2=cbind(lon_destino, lat_destino))/1000))

We split the original dataset into takeoff and landing records. This allows us to match many of the flights and obtain their flight times.

In the info_vuelos table, we calculate the distance traveled, median flight time, and average flight speed for the matched flights. In the example below, the distance from EZE (Ezeiza) to BAR (Bariloche) is 1,434 km, and the median flight time is almost 2 hours (1.88). From these values, we estimate an average flight speed of approximately 761 km/h.

To better understand the results, we produce a statistical summary and a boxplot:

summary(info_vuelos$velocidad_de_vuelo_kmH)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   105.0   344.2   481.1   484.5   621.2   891.5
boxplot(info_vuelos$velocidad_de_vuelo_kmH, ylab="Velocidad de vuelo en km x hr", main="Boxplot de velocidades de vuelos")
abline(h = mean(info_vuelos$velocidad_de_vuelo_kmH), col='orange')

Figure 1.3: Boxplot of flight speed in km/h

Figure 1.3 shows a median speed of 481 km/h, with most flights traveling at speeds between 344 km/h and 621 km/h.

2 Part Two: a comparison of 2015 and 2019

Assignment instructions

  • Explore the data using the tools you have learned. Formulate questions that interest you and develop hypotheses that might answer them, drawing on the measures and visualizations covered in class.

  • Report your questions and hypotheses, aiming to build a narrative. Combine text, code, and visualizations.

Suggestion for Part Two: Consider each variable and the information it provides, and think about how to summarize and visualize it. Then consider each possible pair of variables and explore their relationship. Summarize and visualize the pairs you find most interesting.

obtener_csv <- function(anio) {
  nombre <- paste0("aterrizajes-y-despegues-registrados-por-eana-", anio, ".csv")
  archivo <- file.path(dir_datos, nombre)
  if (!file.exists(archivo)) {
    message("Descargando datos de ", anio, "...")
    temporal <- tempfile(pattern=paste0("vuelos_", anio, "_"), tmpdir=dir_datos)
    on.exit(unlink(temporal), add=TRUE)
    estado <- tryCatch(
      utils::download.file(paste0(url_datos, nombre), temporal,
                           mode="wb", method="libcurl", quiet=FALSE),
      error=function(e) stop(
        "No se pudo descargar ", nombre, ". Extraé el ZIP completo junto al Rmd. Detalle: ",
        conditionMessage(e), call.=FALSE)
    )
    if (estado != 0L || !file.exists(temporal)) {
      stop("La descarga no se completó: ", nombre, call.=FALSE)
    }
    if (unname(tools::md5sum(temporal)) != unname(md5_esperados[as.character(anio)])) {
      stop("El archivo descargado está incompleto o difiere de la copia verificada: ",
           nombre, call.=FALSE)
    }
    if (!file.rename(temporal, archivo)) {
      stop("No se pudo guardar el CSV en ", dir_datos, call.=FALSE)
    }
  }
  archivo
}

Introduction

This project was motivated by the group's prior knowledge of changes in Argentina's commercial aviation sector between 2015 and 2019, including airport openings, the emergence of low-cost airlines, and a more diverse flight market. We sought to explore and quantify these changes using the available data.

We examine how the number of scheduled non-international departures changed between 2015 and 2020. We use the same selection criteria for every year and keep a record of the rows retained.

# No exigimos coordenadas ni tipo de aeronave para contar vuelos.
# Los faltantes geográficos se tratan después, en el análisis que los necesita.
leer_vuelos <- function(anio) {
  archivo <- obtener_csv(anio)
  originales <- read.csv(
    archivo, fileEncoding = "latin1", sep = ";", strip.white = TRUE,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  requeridas <- c("Fecha", "Clase.de.Vuelo", "Clasificación.Vuelo",
                 "Tipo.de.Movimiento", "Origen.OACI", "Destino.OACI",
                 "Aerolinea.Nombre")
  if (!all(requeridas %in% names(originales))) {
    stop("Faltan columnas en ", archivo, ": ",
         paste(setdiff(requeridas, names(originales)), collapse = ", "))
  }
  originales <- originales %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(trimws(.x), "")))
  originales$Fecha <- as.Date(originales$Fecha, format = "%d/%m/%Y")

  despegues <- originales %>%
    filter(Clasificación.Vuelo != "Internacional",
           Clase.de.Vuelo == "Regular",
           Tipo.de.Movimiento == "Despegue")
  datos <- despegues %>%
    filter(!is.na(Aerolinea.Nombre), Aerolinea.Nombre != "N/A") %>%
    mutate(Aerolinea.Nombre = case_when(
      str_detect(Aerolinea.Nombre, "LATAM") ~ "LATAM",
      str_detect(Aerolinea.Nombre, "LADE") ~ "LADE",
      str_detect(Aerolinea.Nombre, "Norwegian") ~ "Norwegian",
      str_detect(Aerolinea.Nombre, "Gol") ~ "Gol",
      str_detect(Aerolinea.Nombre, "Azul") ~ "Azul Linhas Aéreas",
      TRUE ~ Aerolinea.Nombre
    ))
  control <- tibble(
    anio = anio,
    filas_originales = nrow(originales),
    despegues_regulares_no_internacionales = nrow(despegues),
    sin_aerolinea_identificada = nrow(despegues) - nrow(datos),
    vuelos_retenidos = nrow(datos),
    fechas_faltantes_retenidas = sum(is.na(datos$Fecha))
  )
  list(datos = datos, control = control)
}

# Formato para que las cifras del texto se actualicen al ejecutar el informe.
fmt_num <- function(x) {
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ".", decimal.mark = ",")
}
fmt_pct <- function(x) {
  ifelse(is.na(x), "no calculable", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1,
                                            decimal.mark = ","))
}

anios <- 2015:2020
# Conservamos las filas de 2015 y 2019; para los demás años solo
# necesitamos el resumen anual. Así se reduce el uso de memoria.
cargas <- list()
controles <- vector("list", length(anios))
for (i in seq_along(anios)) {
  carga <- leer_vuelos(anios[i])
  controles[[i]] <- carga$control
  if (anios[i] %in% c(2015, 2019)) cargas[[as.character(anios[i])]] <- carga
}
rm(carga)
control_lectura <- bind_rows(controles)
control_lectura
vuelos_por_anio <- control_lectura %>%
  select(anio, n = vuelos_retenidos)

ggplot(vuelos_por_anio, aes(x = as.factor(anio), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  ggtitle("Cantidad de vuelos por año") +
  xlab("") + ylab("Cantidad de despegues") + theme_minimal()

Scheduled non-international departures by year

The annual chart provides an overview of changes over time. The following analysis focuses on 2015 and 2019; 2020 serves as a reference for the beginning of the pandemic.

We set out to analyze changes in flights between 2015 and 2019 and in Argentina's commercial flight network. We begin by comparing flight counts, the main airlines operating those flights, and their destination regions. This allows us to assess whether the supplied datasets support the hypothesis of changes during this period.

The study considers the following:

  1. the number of flights in 2015 and 2019
  2. flight connections in 2015 and 2019
  3. the airlines operating those flights.

We examine several geographic scales: national, regional, provincial, and local.

Loading the data

We add city, province, and coordinate information from a historical revision of Wikipedia, dated 2021-08-03. The table is included in this file so that it remains unchanged across runs. We cannot guarantee that this is the exact revision used in the original submission.

tabla_aeropuerto <- read.csv(text=texto_aeropuertos, stringsAsFactors=FALSE,
                             check.names=FALSE)
names(tabla_aeropuerto) <- str_squish(names(tabla_aeropuerto))
if (!all(c("City served", "Province", "ICAO", "Coordinates") %in%
         names(tabla_aeropuerto))) stop("La copia de aeropuertos no tiene las columnas esperadas.")

# Usamos la representación decimal; no interpretamos minutos y segundos como decimales.
extraer_coordenadas <- function(x) {
  texto <- str_squish(str_replace(x, "^.*?/\\s*", ""))
  hemisferios <- str_match(
    texto, "([0-9]+(?:\\.[0-9]+)?)\\s*°?\\s*([NS])\\s*[,;]?\\s+([0-9]+(?:\\.[0-9]+)?)\\s*°?\\s*([EW])"
  )
  lat <- as.numeric(hemisferios[, 2]) * ifelse(hemisferios[, 3] == "S", -1, 1)
  lon <- as.numeric(hemisferios[, 4]) * ifelse(hemisferios[, 5] == "W", -1, 1)
  # Algunas versiones muestran el par decimal con signos, separado por punto y coma.
  par <- str_match(texto, "^\\s*([+-]?[0-9]+(?:\\.[0-9]+)?)\\s*;\\s*([+-]?[0-9]+(?:\\.[0-9]+)?)")
  faltan <- is.na(lat) | is.na(lon)
  lat[faltan] <- as.numeric(par[faltan, 2])
  lon[faltan] <- as.numeric(par[faltan, 3])
  invalidas <- (!is.na(lat) & abs(lat) > 90) | (!is.na(lon) & abs(lon) > 180)
  lat[invalidas] <- NA_real_
  lon[invalidas] <- NA_real_
  tibble(lat = lat, lon = lon)
}

info_aeropuerto <- tabla_aeropuerto %>%
  transmute(
    Codigo.OACI = str_trim(str_remove_all(ICAO, "\\[[^]]*\\]")),
    Ciudad = na_if(str_squish(`City served`), ""),
    Provincia = na_if(str_squish(Province), ""),
    Coordenadas = Coordinates
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Codigo.OACI), str_detect(Codigo.OACI, "^[A-Z]{4}$")) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  mutate(Ciudad = case_when(
    Ciudad == "Buenos Aires metropolitan area" ~ "AMBA",
    Ciudad == "Catamarca (San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca)" ~ "Catamarca",
    Ciudad == "Jujuy (San Salvador de Jujuy)" ~ "Jujuy",
    Ciudad == "Tucumán (San Miguel de Tucumán)" ~ "Tucumán",
    Ciudad == "San Fernando (San Fernando de la Buena Vista)" ~ "San Fernando",
    TRUE ~ Ciudad
  ))
if (anyDuplicated(info_aeropuerto$Codigo.OACI)) {
  repetidos <- info_aeropuerto$Codigo.OACI[duplicated(info_aeropuerto$Codigo.OACI)]
  stop("Hay códigos OACI con más de una fila: ", paste(unique(repetidos), collapse = ", "))
}
info_aeropuerto <- bind_cols(info_aeropuerto,
                             extraer_coordenadas(info_aeropuerto$Coordenadas))

agregar_aeropuertos <- function(datos) {
  salida <- datos %>%
    left_join(info_aeropuerto %>% transmute(
      Origen.OACI = Codigo.OACI, Ciudad.Origen = Ciudad,
      Provincia.Origen = Provincia, lat_origen = lat, lon_origen = lon
    ), by = "Origen.OACI") %>%
    left_join(info_aeropuerto %>% transmute(
      Destino.OACI = Codigo.OACI, Ciudad.Destino = Ciudad,
      Provincia.Destino = Provincia, lat_destino = lat, lon_destino = lon
    ), by = "Destino.OACI")
  if (nrow(salida) != nrow(datos)) stop("La unión de aeropuertos multiplicó filas.")
  salida
}

datos_2015 <- agregar_aeropuertos(cargas[["2015"]]$datos)
datos_2019 <- agregar_aeropuertos(cargas[["2019"]]$datos)

control_geografia <- bind_rows(
  lapply(c(2015, 2019), function(anio) {
    datos <- if (anio == 2015) datos_2015 else datos_2019
    tibble(
      anio = anio, vuelos = nrow(datos),
      sin_ciudad_origen = sum(is.na(datos$Ciudad.Origen)),
      sin_ciudad_destino = sum(is.na(datos$Ciudad.Destino)),
      sin_provincia_origen = sum(is.na(datos$Provincia.Origen)),
      sin_provincia_destino = sum(is.na(datos$Provincia.Destino)),
      sin_coordenadas_completas = sum(!complete.cases(
        datos[c("lat_origen", "lon_origen", "lat_destino", "lon_destino")]
      ))
    )
  })
)
control_geografia

National counts retain flights even when geographic information is missing. Regional comparisons require the relevant province; city-to-city connections require both cities. Complete coordinates are required only for the route map. Cases with missing information are recorded in the preceding checks.

Flights at the national level

We first examine the routes recorded in the two years under study:

v_2015 <- datos_2015 %>% 
  filter(!is.na(Origen.OACI), !is.na(Destino.OACI),
         Origen.OACI != Destino.OACI) %>%
  select(Origen.OACI, Destino.OACI, Ciudad.Origen, Ciudad.Destino,
         lat_origen, lon_origen, lat_destino, lon_destino) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  drop_na(lat_origen, lon_origen, lat_destino, lon_destino) %>%
  filter(lat_origen != lat_destino | lon_origen != lon_destino) %>% 
  mutate(anio="2015") %>% 
  as_tibble() 

v_2019 <- datos_2019 %>% 
  filter(!is.na(Origen.OACI), !is.na(Destino.OACI),
         Origen.OACI != Destino.OACI) %>%
  select(Origen.OACI, Destino.OACI, Ciudad.Origen, Ciudad.Destino,
         lat_origen, lon_origen, lat_destino, lon_destino) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  drop_na(lat_origen, lon_origen, lat_destino, lon_destino) %>%
  filter(lat_origen != lat_destino | lon_origen != lon_destino) %>% 
  mutate(anio="2019") %>% 
  as_tibble() 

v_tot <- rbind(v_2015, v_2019)

mapa_arg <- ggplot() +
  borders(database = "world", regions = c("argentina"), fill = 'grey13') 

mapa_arg +
  geom_point(data=v_tot, 
             aes(x=lon_origen, y=lat_origen), 
             size=.3, 
             col="chocolate1") +
  geom_point(data=v_tot, 
             aes(x=lon_destino, y=lat_destino),
             size=.3, 
             col="chocolate1") +
  geom_curve(data = v_tot, 
             aes(x= lon_origen, y=lat_origen, xend=lon_destino, yend=lat_destino, col=anio),
             size=.1,
             curvature=.06) +
  labs(col="año") +
  theme_void()

The map shows the routes recorded in each year, allowing us to identify shared connections and routes that appear in only one of the two periods. Each curve represents a route, not its flight frequency.

We then examine how many flights were recorded in each year:

cant_vuelos_2015 <-  datos_2015 %>% 
  count(sort=T) %>% 
  mutate(anio = "2015" )

cant_vuelos_2019 <-  datos_2019 %>% 
  count(sort=T) %>% 
  mutate(anio = "2019" )

cant_vuelos_totales <- rbind(cant_vuelos_2015, cant_vuelos_2019) 

ggplot(cant_vuelos_totales, aes(x= anio, y=n)) +
  geom_bar(stat='identity', position='dodge') +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylab("Cantidad de vuelos") +
  xlab("") +
  ggtitle("Cantidad de vuelos en el 2015 y 2019") +
   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust=1), plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

Number of flights in 2015 and 2019

We retained 73,688 departures in 2015 and 117,497 in 2019, a change of 59.5%. Next, we examine how this change was distributed across regions.

Flights at the regional level

For this analysis, we divide Argentina into five main regions: Cuyo, Buenos Aires, Patagonia, North, and Central, as shown in the map below. We add a column containing this regional classification.

Regional map (original geographic labels in Spanish)

Map labels: Norte Grande, North; Centro, Central; Nuevo Cuyo, Cuyo; Patagónica, Patagonia.

vec_norte <- c("Salta", "Formosa", "Tucumán", "Chaco", "Jujuy", "Misiones",
               "Catamarca", "Corrientes", "Santiago del Estero")
asignar_region <- function(provincia) {
  case_when(
    provincia %in% c("San Juan", "Mendoza", "La Rioja", "San Luis") ~ "Cuyo",
    provincia %in% c("Buenos Aires", "Buenos Aires City", "Autonomous City of Buenos Aires",
                     "Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires", "CABA") ~ "Buenos Aires",
    provincia %in% c("Chubut", "Río Negro", "Santa Cruz", "Tierra del Fuego",
                     "Neuquén", "La Pampa") ~ "Patagonia",
    provincia %in% vec_norte ~ "Norte",
    provincia %in% c("Córdoba", "Santa Fe", "Entre Ríos") ~ "Centro",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
}
datos_2015 <- datos_2015 %>% mutate(
  Region.Origen = asignar_region(Provincia.Origen),
  Region.Destino = asignar_region(Provincia.Destino)
)
datos_2019 <- datos_2019 %>% mutate(
  Region.Origen = asignar_region(Provincia.Origen),
  Region.Destino = asignar_region(Provincia.Destino)
)
control_regiones <- bind_rows(
  datos_2015 %>% summarise(anio = 2015,
    sin_region_origen = sum(is.na(Region.Origen)),
    sin_region_destino = sum(is.na(Region.Destino))),
  datos_2019 %>% summarise(anio = 2019,
    sin_region_origen = sum(is.na(Region.Origen)),
    sin_region_destino = sum(is.na(Region.Destino)))
)
control_regiones
cant_vxRegion_2015 <-  datos_2015 %>% 
  filter(!is.na(Region.Origen)) %>%
  group_by(Region.Origen) %>% 
  count(sort=T) %>% 
  mutate(anio = "2015" )

cant_vxRegion_2019 <-  datos_2019 %>% 
  filter(!is.na(Region.Origen)) %>%
  group_by(Region.Origen) %>% 
  count(sort=T) %>% 
  mutate(anio = "2019" )

cant_vxRegion <- rbind(cant_vxRegion_2015, cant_vxRegion_2019) 

ggplot(cant_vxRegion, aes(x=reorder(Region.Origen,-n), y=n, fill=anio)) +
  geom_bar(stat='identity', position='dodge') +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylab("Cantidad de vuelos") +
  xlab("") +
  labs(fill = "año") +
  ggtitle("Cantidad de vuelos por región en el 2015 y 2019") +
   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust=1), plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

Number of flights by region in 2015 and 2019

The regional chart compares departures by region of origin. The following table quantifies the changes. Flights with an unidentified region of origin are excluded from this comparison but retained in the national total.

t_2015 <- cant_vxRegion_2015 %>% 
  select(-c(anio)) %>% 
  rename(vuelos_2015 = n)

t_2019 <- cant_vxRegion_2019 %>% 
  select(-c(anio)) %>% 
  rename(vuelos_2019 =n)

t_dif_regiones <- full_join(t_2015, t_2019, by="Region.Origen") %>% 
  mutate(vuelos_2015 = replace_na(vuelos_2015, 0L),
         vuelos_2019 = replace_na(vuelos_2019, 0L),
         dif_porcentual = ifelse(vuelos_2015 > 0,
           100 * (vuelos_2019 - vuelos_2015) / vuelos_2015, NA_real_)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(dif_porcentual)) 
t_dif_regiones

Central had the largest calculable percentage change, at 88.1%. The table allows us to compare this relative change with each region's flight count. When a region has no flights recorded in 2015, its percentage change is left missing because there is no positive baseline from which to calculate it.

These results lead us to examine how flight counts changed in the North region: whether the change was uniform across provinces or whether some stood out.

Flights at the provincial and local levels

# Contamos despegues por provincia de origen del Norte.
# Cada fila retenida representa un despegue y se cuenta una sola vez.
datos_norte_2015 <- datos_2015 %>% 
  filter(Region.Origen == "Norte")
datos_norte_2019 <- datos_2019 %>% 
  filter(Region.Origen=="Norte")
cant_vxProv_2015 <-  datos_norte_2015 %>% 
  group_by(Provincia.Origen) %>% 
  count(sort=T) %>% 
  mutate(anio = "2015" )

cant_vxProv_2019 <-  datos_norte_2019 %>% 
  group_by(Provincia.Origen) %>% 
  count(sort=T) %>% 
  mutate(anio = "2019" )

cant_vxProv <- rbind(cant_vxProv_2015, cant_vxProv_2019)

ggplot(cant_vxProv, aes(x=reorder(Provincia.Origen,-n), y=n, fill=anio)) +
  geom_bar(stat='identity', position='dodge') +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylab("Cantidad de vuelos") +
  xlab("") +
  labs(fill = "año") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust=1))

Number of flights by province in the North region

The provincial chart shows departure counts by province. We also calculate percentage changes to distinguish the scale of operations from their relative change.

t_2015 <- cant_vxProv_2015 %>% 
  select(-c(anio)) %>% 
  rename(vuelos_2015 = n)

t_2019 <- cant_vxProv_2019 %>% 
  select(-c(anio)) %>% 
  rename(vuelos_2019 =n)

t_dif_prov <- full_join(t_2015, t_2019, by="Provincia.Origen") %>% 
  mutate(vuelos_2015 = replace_na(vuelos_2015, 0L),
         vuelos_2019 = replace_na(vuelos_2019, 0L),
         dif_porcentual = ifelse(vuelos_2015 > 0,
           100 * (vuelos_2019 - vuelos_2015) / vuelos_2015, NA_real_)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(dif_porcentual)) 
t_dif_prov

Corrientes recorded 65 departures in 2015 and 706 in 2019, a change of 986.2%. A large percentage change should be interpreted alongside the initial flight count. The proximity of Corrientes and Resistencia may be relevant when interpreting their activity, although these data do not establish that one substituted for the other.

In Formosa, the change was 15.6%, compared with a provincial median of 77.4%. The difference from that median was -61.8 percentage points (Formosa minus the median).

##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   15.55   70.52   77.37  171.88   93.23  986.15

City connectivity in the North region

After comparing flight counts, we ask whether connectivity changed for cities in the North region. We construct graphs using routes with at least one endpoint in this region. Each node represents a city, and each edge indicates that at least one flight between two cities was recorded in the year under study. We use a simple undirected graph, counting one connection per city pair even when flights operate in both directions. Each node's degree is therefore the number of distinct cities to which it is connected within this set of routes.

# Para estudiar conexiones necesitamos conocer ambas ciudades y poder
# identificar al menos uno de los extremos como perteneciente al Norte.
datos_rutas_norte_2015 <- datos_2015 %>%
  filter(Region.Origen %in% "Norte" | Region.Destino %in% "Norte") %>%
  drop_na(Ciudad.Origen, Ciudad.Destino)

edges_2015_norte <- datos_rutas_norte_2015 %>%
  select(Ciudad.Origen, Ciudad.Destino) %>%
  filter(Ciudad.Origen != Ciudad.Destino) %>%
  distinct()

datos_rutas_norte_2019 <- datos_2019 %>%
  filter(Region.Origen %in% "Norte" | Region.Destino %in% "Norte") %>%
  drop_na(Ciudad.Origen, Ciudad.Destino)

edges_2019_norte <- datos_rutas_norte_2019 %>%
  select(Ciudad.Origen, Ciudad.Destino) %>%
  filter(Ciudad.Origen != Ciudad.Destino) %>%
  distinct()
# Al hacer el grafo no dirigido, A-B y B-A pueden quedar como aristas
# paralelas. simplify elimina esa duplicación antes de calcular el grado.
g_2015 <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(edges_2015_norte, directed=FALSE) %>%
  igraph::simplify(remove.multiple=TRUE, remove.loops=TRUE)
g_2015 <- igraph::set_vertex_attr(
  g_2015, "grado", value=igraph::degree(g_2015, loops=FALSE)
) %>%
  as_tbl_graph()

g_2019 <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(edges_2019_norte, directed=FALSE) %>%
  igraph::simplify(remove.multiple=TRUE, remove.loops=TRUE)
g_2019 <- igraph::set_vertex_attr(
  g_2019, "grado", value=igraph::degree(g_2019, loops=FALSE)
) %>%
  as_tbl_graph()

# Los gráficos interactivos usarán las mismas aristas que estos grafos.
# Los nombres Origen/Destino aquí identifican los extremos de cada arista;
# no indican una dirección del vuelo en este grafo no dirigido.
edges_2015_norte <- igraph::as_data_frame(g_2015, what="edges") %>%
  rename(Ciudad.Origen=from, Ciudad.Destino=to)
edges_2019_norte <- igraph::as_data_frame(g_2019, what="edges") %>%
  rename(Ciudad.Origen=from, Ciudad.Destino=to)

p_2015 <- g_2015 %>%
  ggraph(layout='linear', circular=TRUE) +
  geom_edge_arc(edge_width=.5, alpha=.4) +
  geom_node_point(aes(color=name, size=grado), show.legend=FALSE) +
  ggtitle("2015") +
  theme_graph(base_family="sans")

p_2015 <- p_2015 +
  geom_node_text(aes(label=name),
                 nudge_x=p_2015$data$x * .2,
                 nudge_y=p_2015$data$y * .2,
                 size=2)

p_2019 <- g_2019 %>%
  ggraph(layout='linear', circular=TRUE) +
  geom_edge_arc(edge_width=.5, alpha=.4) +
  geom_node_point(aes(color=name, size=grado), show.legend=FALSE) +
  ggtitle("2019") +
  theme_graph(base_family="sans")

p_2019 <- p_2019 +
  geom_node_text(aes(label=name),
                 nudge_x=p_2019$data$x * .2,
                 nudge_y=p_2019$data$y * .2,
                 size=2)

grid.arrange(p_2015, p_2019, ncol=2)

The following interactive graph shows the connections of each city in 2015:

simpleNetwork(edges_2015_norte,
              Source="Ciudad.Origen",
              Target="Ciudad.Destino",
              linkDistance=90,
              fontSize=10,
              charge=-80,
              nodeColour="#F8766D",
              zoom=FALSE)

The next graph shows the connections in 2019:

simpleNetwork(edges_2019_norte,
              Source="Ciudad.Origen",
              Target="Ciudad.Destino",
              linkDistance=90,
              fontSize=10,
              nodeColour="#619CFF",
              charge=-70,
              zoom=FALSE)

The following tables show the ten cities with the most connections within this subgraph. They include both cities in the North and cities in other regions connected to it, so they are not rankings restricted to northern cities. Ties in degree are broken alphabetically by city name.

conectividad_2015 <- g_2015 %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  select(name, grado) %>%
  arrange(desc(grado), name)

tConectividad_2015 <- conectividad_2015 %>%
  head(10) %>%
  rename("Ciudades 2015"=name)
tConectividad_2015
conectividad_2019 <- g_2019 %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  select(name, grado) %>%
  arrange(desc(grado), name)

tConectividad_2019 <- conectividad_2019 %>%
  head(10) %>%
  rename("Ciudades 2019"=name)
tConectividad_2019

Flight flows from cities in the North region

In addition to counting connections, we examine how many flights operate on each route. We select up to ten cities in the North based on their number of connections. We first restrict the ranking to cities in this region, then select those with the highest degree, breaking ties by name. Selection is performed separately for each year, so the cities shown may differ.

# Identificamos las ciudades del Norte usando ambos extremos de los vuelos.
ciudades_norte_2015 <- bind_rows(
  datos_rutas_norte_2015 %>%
    filter(Region.Origen %in% "Norte") %>%
    transmute(name=Ciudad.Origen),
  datos_rutas_norte_2015 %>%
    filter(Region.Destino %in% "Norte") %>%
    transmute(name=Ciudad.Destino)
) %>%
  distinct(name)

ciudades_norte_2019 <- bind_rows(
  datos_rutas_norte_2019 %>%
    filter(Region.Origen %in% "Norte") %>%
    transmute(name=Ciudad.Origen),
  datos_rutas_norte_2019 %>%
    filter(Region.Destino %in% "Norte") %>%
    transmute(name=Ciudad.Destino)
) %>%
  distinct(name)

tConectividadNorte_2015 <- conectividad_2015 %>%
  semi_join(ciudades_norte_2015, by="name") %>%
  arrange(desc(grado), name) %>%
  head(10)

tConectividadNorte_2019 <- conectividad_2019 %>%
  semi_join(ciudades_norte_2019, by="name") %>%
  arrange(desc(grado), name) %>%
  head(10)

# Para los flujos volvemos a los registros de vuelos: conservamos su
# dirección y contamos todos los despegues, no las aristas del grafo simple.
v_salida_norte_2015 <- datos_rutas_norte_2015 %>%
  filter(Region.Origen %in% "Norte",
         Ciudad.Origen %in% tConectividadNorte_2015$name,
         Ciudad.Origen != Ciudad.Destino)

v_salida_norte_2019 <- datos_rutas_norte_2019 %>%
  filter(Region.Origen %in% "Norte",
         Ciudad.Origen %in% tConectividadNorte_2019$name,
         Ciudad.Origen != Ciudad.Destino)

In the Sankey diagrams, origin cities are on the left and their destinations are on the right. The width of each band represents the number of flights in that direction.

# Las filas son ciudades de origen y las columnas, ciudades de destino.
data <- table(v_salida_norte_2015$Ciudad.Origen,
              v_salida_norte_2015$Ciudad.Destino) %>%
  as.data.frame.matrix()

links <- data %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var="source") %>%
  gather(key="target", value="value", -1) %>%
  mutate(target=tolower(target)) %>%
  filter(value != 0)

# Los destinos se escriben en minúscula para mantener separados los nodos
# de origen y destino cuando una ciudad aparece a ambos lados del diagrama.
nodes <- data.frame(
  name=unique(c(as.character(links$source), as.character(links$target)))
)
links$IDsource <- match(links$source, nodes$name) - 1
links$IDtarget <- match(links$target, nodes$name) - 1

sankeyNetwork(Links=links, Nodes=nodes,
              Source="IDsource",
              Target="IDtarget",
              Value="value",
              NodeID="name",
              fontSize=12,
              nodeWidth=40)

Flights from the selected cities in the North in 2015

Note: To see the number of flights from one city to another, hover over the relevant band for a few seconds.

data <- table(v_salida_norte_2019$Ciudad.Origen,
              v_salida_norte_2019$Ciudad.Destino) %>%
  as.data.frame.matrix()

links <- data %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var="source") %>%
  gather(key="target", value="value", -1) %>%
  mutate(target=tolower(target)) %>%
  filter(value != 0)

nodes <- data.frame(
  name=unique(c(as.character(links$source), as.character(links$target)))
)
links$IDsource <- match(links$source, nodes$name) - 1
links$IDtarget <- match(links$target, nodes$name) - 1

sankeyNetwork(Links=links, Nodes=nodes,
              Source="IDsource",
              Target="IDtarget",
              Value="value",
              NodeID="name",
              fontSize=12,
              nodeWidth=40)

Flights from the selected cities in the North in 2019

Airlines with the most flights nationwide in 2015 and 2019

We next analyze airlines, focusing on the five with the most scheduled non-international departures in each year and comparing their composition. These national counts do not require airport cities or coordinates, so we retain flights even when that information is missing.

cant_vxAerolineas_2015 <- datos_2015 %>%
  count(Aerolinea.Nombre, name="n") %>%
  arrange(desc(n), Aerolinea.Nombre)

filtro_top_5_2015 <- cant_vxAerolineas_2015 %>%
  head(5) %>%
  pull(Aerolinea.Nombre)

datos_top5_2015 <- datos_2015 %>%
  filter(Aerolinea.Nombre %in% filtro_top_5_2015)

cant_vxAerolineas_2019 <- datos_2019 %>%
  count(Aerolinea.Nombre, name="n") %>%
  arrange(desc(n), Aerolinea.Nombre)

filtro_top_5_2019 <- cant_vxAerolineas_2019 %>%
  head(5) %>%
  pull(Aerolinea.Nombre)

datos_top5_2019 <- datos_2019 %>%
  filter(Aerolinea.Nombre %in% filtro_top_5_2019)
rbind(datos_top5_2015 %>% mutate(anio=2015),
      datos_top5_2019 %>% mutate(anio=2019)) %>%
  count(anio, Aerolinea.Nombre, name="n") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=factor(anio), y=n, fill=Aerolinea.Nombre)) +
  geom_col(position="fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=function(x) paste0(round(100*x), "%")) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette="Set2") +
  labs(x="Año", y="Proporción de vuelos dentro del top 5", fill="Aerolínea") +
  theme_minimal()

Distribution of flights among the five leading airlines nationwide in each year

Quantitative analysis

In the tables, n is each airline's flight count, and pct_vuelos_top5 is its percentage of the total flights operated by the five airlines selected for that year. This denominator excludes other airlines, so these percentages do not represent shares of the overall market.

2015

tParticipacion_top5_2015 <- datos_top5_2015 %>%
  count(Aerolinea.Nombre, name="n") %>%
  mutate(pct_vuelos_top5=round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n), Aerolinea.Nombre)

tParticipacion_top5_2015

2019

tParticipacion_top5_2019 <- datos_top5_2019 %>%
  count(Aerolinea.Nombre, name="n") %>%
  mutate(pct_vuelos_top5=round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n), Aerolinea.Nombre)

tParticipacion_top5_2019

The selected airlines account for 73,017 flights in 2015 and 109,795 in 2019. Comparing names, counts, and percentages helps distinguish changes in the composition of this group from changes in flight volume. A change in relative share does not, by itself, imply that an airline increased or decreased its flight count.

National top-five airlines with flights linked to the North

Returning to the North region, we analyze flights originating or ending there, retaining the five airlines selected nationally for each year. This is therefore not a new ranking of the five leading airlines in the North. We include records in which at least one endpoint can be identified as belonging to this region.

datos_top5Norte_2015 <- datos_top5_2015 %>%
  filter(Region.Origen %in% "Norte" | Region.Destino %in% "Norte") %>%
  select(Aerolinea.Nombre) %>%
  mutate(anio=2015)

datos_top5Norte_2019 <- datos_top5_2019 %>%
  filter(Region.Origen %in% "Norte" | Region.Destino %in% "Norte") %>%
  select(Aerolinea.Nombre) %>%
  mutate(anio=2019)

df_vuelosAerolineas <- rbind(datos_top5Norte_2015, datos_top5Norte_2019)

df_vuelosAerolineas %>%
  count(anio, Aerolinea.Nombre, name="n") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=factor(anio), y=n, fill=Aerolinea.Nombre)) +
  geom_col(position="fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=function(x) paste0(round(100*x), "%")) +
  labs(x="Año", y="Proporción entre las aerolíneas seleccionadas", fill="Aerolínea") +
  theme_minimal()

National top-five airlines: distribution of their flights linked to the North in each year

In these tables, pct_vuelos_top5_nacional_en_norte uses only the flights linked to the North operated by the national top-five airlines for each year as its denominator. We also retain n to compare counts.

2015

tParticipacion_Norte_2015 <- datos_top5Norte_2015 %>%
  count(Aerolinea.Nombre, name="n") %>%
  mutate(pct_vuelos_top5_nacional_en_norte=round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n), Aerolinea.Nombre)

tParticipacion_Norte_2015

2019

tParticipacion_Norte_2019 <- datos_top5Norte_2019 %>%
  count(Aerolinea.Nombre, name="n") %>%
  mutate(pct_vuelos_top5_nacional_en_norte=round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n), Aerolinea.Nombre)

tParticipacion_Norte_2019

Within this selection, 20,553 flights linked to the North were recorded in 2015 and 34,985 in 2019. The tables allow us to compare the observed composition and volumes, but not to attribute their changes to an airline's entry or to other causes.

Final reflections

We analyzed scheduled non-international departures in 2015 and 2019 at several scales: national, regional, provincial, and city-to-city. We also compared connection counts, flight volumes, and the composition of the selected airlines. These measures answer different questions: a city may have more connections without every route having a higher flight frequency.

The results describe the available records. Geographic comparisons depend on the information that could be matched to each airport, while airline percentages refer to the selected groups. This exploratory analysis provides a basis for new questions about the observed changes, but does not establish their causes.
